text:
The circularity of the AI capex problem

If you are worried about supply of fresh equity, why are those companies who benefit from the spend of this new capital being sold?

Why is everyone worried about dilution? Don't these projects have good margins with utility like demand than meta's business as a whole? There is a gap of a few years but tech investors have rarely been worried about things like that before.

The only proper sense bearish take to explain a day like today is that there will be insufficient demand for compute in the future and that all this spending is on a white elephant. I haven't really heard many make this case.

But I think it's the only thing that underlies these sort of moves. People doubt AI fundamentally and when they get asked to make a sacrifice for it (handing out capital), they flinch. It's not going to work, there's not enough demand. This makes selling across the AI supply chain rational.

Companies like coreweave are the ultimate expression of this. Individually unimportant in the whole scheme of things being opportunistic extremely highly leveraged (not just financially either, but to input pricing and execution risk) players that will just have their supply absorbed by someone else if they fail. There pricing offers a barometer in the belief in this future demand.

So, it's all just sentiment. And this makes sense. It's an enormous bet on something that is doubted by and is frightening to many and is many years into the future. Much harder than selling ads now.

AI has to generate enough economic productivity to pay for itself and the margins that justify these capital raises in the first place. I think it will. I don't think most agree and they are just getting pulled along as beta.

Even if it is successful in generating enough productivity to pay for itself (plus some juicy inference margin) you have many that are frightened of it in addition to doubting it. The corporate factory line worker is at risk just like they were to machines in the industrial revolution. This will prompt a response from government. How do you price that? By discounting the ROI on these investments?

This would get you to the point of being worried about dilution. The trade is just too uncertain and needs so much capital that the only realistic way it fails in the medium term is that we become forever compute constrained and AI has a small percentage of the effect it could've had, taking down the labs with it.

The New Humanity

A Dialogue from the Global Council

ELITIST: You still believe we want people to love one another?

CITIZEN: Isn’t that what you tell us? Unity. Diversity. A world without borders.

ELITIST: Unity is a useful slogan. What we actually want is uniformity. People who eat the same food, watch the same programs, speak the same approved language, and have forgotten why their grandparents ever fought to preserve anything.

CITIZEN: You want us to abandon our cultures?

ELITIST: Abandon? No. We want you to turn them into merchandise. Sell the costumes. Celebrate the festivals. Put the old traditions on television between advertisements. Keep the decorations; discard the convictions.

CITIZEN: And mixing every culture together will somehow make us easier to govern?

ELITIST: A population without a common memory is a population without a common purpose. Give people a thousand identities, a million distractions, and a thousand reasons to distrust their neighbors. Then offer them one authority capable of managing the chaos.

CITIZEN: So you manufacture the problem and sell yourselves as the solution.

ELITIST: Now you’re learning.

CITIZEN: And what happens to the people who refuse?

ELITIST: They become inconvenient. We call them backward, intolerant, or dangerous. We don’t need to silence every dissenter. We merely need to make dissent socially expensive.

CITIZEN: And the ruling class? Will your children live under the same system?

ELITIST: Of course not. Our children will attend the finest schools, live behind secure gates, and inherit the institutions that manage everyone else’s lives.

CITIZEN: Then this isn’t equality. It’s an aristocracy wearing the mask of progress.

ELITIST: Every age has its aristocracy. The clever ones simply learn to call theirs something more appealing.

CITIZEN: And what do you call yours?

ELITIST: Global governance. Sustainable development. Human cooperation. Choose whichever phrase makes you sleep best.

CITIZEN: One world, ruled by a few.

ELITIST: Precisely. And the beautiful part is that the public will argue endlessly about the slogans while we consolidate the power.

CITIZEN: You think people are too stupid to see what you’re doing.

ELITIST: No. I think people are too busy, too divided, and too exhausted to do anything about it.

CITIZEN: And if they finally wake up?

ELITIST: Then we will tell them that the world is too complicated to run without us.

The Citizen looks through the glass wall at the city below: a thousand flags in the museums, a thousand languages fading from the streets, and one enormous emblem glowing above the government tower.

CITIZEN: You haven’t united humanity.

ELITIST: What have we done, then?

CITIZEN: You’ve made the whole world a kingdom—and convinced the people they elected the king.

For the first time, the Elitist says nothing.

Kent, the bible doesn't say that Cain "brought the fruit of the ground" .  The KJV says "brought of the fruit of the ground". Cain’s Offering: Fruit on the Ground

Genesis 4:3 describes Cain’s offering with an unusual phrase: **מִפְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה** (*mipperî hāʾădāmāh*)—“from the fruit of the ground.” My argument is that this wording may describe fruit associated with the ground itself—fruit already lying on Cain’s ground. Cain's ground fits the Hebrew well.
1. The wording is distinctive
The Bible refers to fruit many times. Before that verse, depending on the translation Fruit is mentioned up to 9 time but Genesis 4:3 uses a notably different construction: “fruit of the ground.” That difference deserves interpretive weight. If the author meant ordinary cultivated produce, why describe Cain’s gift this way rather than with the more familiar language used everywhere for fruit in the bible and elsewhere?
The Hebrew phrase unusual wording, used no where else, invites us to ask, is that the reason Cain's offering had no respect?

2. The earlier uses of “fruit” provide a frame of reference
The earlier biblical references to fruit establish a pattern for what “fruit” means and how it is described. Genesis 4:3 should be read in light of that foundation, not as though *perî* automatically means any agricultural produce. The contrast between those earlier descriptions and Cain’s wording may signal that something about his offering was unusual.

3. The offerings are contrasted, and Cain’s is rejected
Abel brings the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions. Cain’s gift is described differently, and the Lord has no respect for it. The passage does not explicitly explain the reason for the rejection, but the contrast makes the nature and quality of Cain’s offering relevant. If his gift consisted of fruit already "sacrificed to" the ground.

4. Fallen fruit is sacrificed by the tree.
If the fruit had fallen from the tree, it could be understood as something the tree had already given up. Cain would then be presenting something already sacrifice by its source, rather than offering a fresh gift of his own. On this reading, it would not function as a genuine sacrifice: something already given up cannot be sacrificed a second time would have no respect from the Lord.

5. The Lord came down and warned Cain. 
The Lord didn't even mention the fruit. The Lord's only concern was how angry Cain was at Abel, that tells us he murdered his brother for an underlying reason, not the Lord's lack of respect.

6. Nowhere in the Bible does fruit come from anywhere except a tree, a womb, a vine, a limb, or a market. 

Conclusion   
Taken together—the one and only use of that Hebrew wording, the earlier biblical pattern for “fruit,” the contrast between Cain’s and Abel’s offerings, Hermeneutics, and Cain’s rejection—these details support that Cain brought fruit already lying on his ground, rather than a fresh, deliberately offered harvest aka a sacrifice. 
This is the only coherent explanation for why Cain’s offering was described differently and was not accepted and the Lord did not mention the fruit to Cain.

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

A degree earned years ago is not a license, and a man who ran a city health department from an office is not the practicing physician voters picture when they hear the title. Letting voters picture someone else is not a rounding error. It is the campaign.
Mike Rogers offers Michigan a record voters can check. El-Sayed offers a biography that dissolves the moment anyone checks it, and a debate performance that started with the claim his own licensing record refutes. If a candidate will stretch the truth about himself in the first five seconds, voters should ask what he will stretch in the United States Senate.

October 22, 2026 | Colorado Front Range

Emergency crews, law enforcement officers, animal control personnel and transportation officials responded to numerous incidents across the Colorado Front Range Thursday afternoon and evening.
